_comment: Rules that read the code rather than the text of it. Each carries one tree-sitter query per language, so teaching a rule about another language is an entry here rather than a change in Rust. What a query cannot express is judgement — whether the argument is a literal, which decides between an ugly call and a dangerous one — and that lives in ast.rs where it can be tested. Captures: @hit is what gets reported, @arg is the argument judged for literalness.

rules.title: Code is built at run time and executed
rules.description: A value decided while the app is running is handed to something that executes it as code.
rules.impact: If any part of that value can be influenced from outside, whoever influences it chooses what the app does next.
rules.fix: Work out what the code is actually for. A lookup table, a match on a fixed set of names, or a small parser will do the job without running text as code.

rules.title: A shell command is built from a value
rules.description: A command line is assembled from something other than fixed text and handed to the shell.
rules.impact: A semicolon or a backtick in the wrong place turns one command into two, and the second one is whatever the attacker wanted.
rules.fix: Pass the program and its arguments as a list instead of a string, so the shell never parses them. Where a shell is genuinely needed, validate the value against a fixed set first.

queries.python:
[(call function: (attribute object: (identifier) @mod attribute: (identifier) @fn)
              arguments: (argument_list . (_) @arg))
       (call function: (identifier) @fn arguments: (argument_list . (_) @arg))] @hit

rules.title: A database query is built by joining text together
rules.description: A query is assembled from pieces rather than sent with its values kept separate.
rules.impact: A quote in someone's name is enough to change what the query does, and a deliberate one can read or delete any table the app can reach.
rules.fix: Send the query with placeholders and pass the values alongside it. Every database library supports this, and it is shorter than building the string.

rules.title: Data from outside is turned back into objects unsafely
rules.description: A format that can describe arbitrary objects is being read with the reader that builds them.
rules.impact: Reading the data is enough to run code: the attacker does not need the app to use the result, only to load it.
rules.fix: Use the safe reader — yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load — and prefer a format that carries data only, such as JSON, for anything that arrives from outside.
